headlines.title: Stocks making the biggest moves midday: MongoDB, Boeing, Kodiak Sciences, Roblox, Nvidia & more
headlines.summary: Here are some of the companies making headlines in midday trading.
headlines.article_text: Stocks making the biggest moves midday: MDB, BA, KOD, RBLX, NVDA Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Here are some of the companies making headlines in midday trading. MongoDB — Shares of the database service provider tanked about 18% following news that CEO CJ Desai is joining Meta as its chief enterprise platform officer, reporting to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg. MongoDB's board named Dev Ittycheria as interim president and CEO. Sweetgreen — The salad chain's stock jumped more than 2% after Wells Fargo upgraded shares to overweight from equal weight and lifted its price target to $11 from $6. Sweetgreen wasn't linked to cyclospora, but Wells Fargo sees headwinds tied to the outbreak subsiding and "transformation initiatives beginning to materialize." Boeing — The aerospace giant's stock tumbled 5%. Over the weekend, Boeing said that it flagged a software glitch last month on some of its 737 Max aircraft that could affect certain landing procedures. U.S. airlines told CNBC they don't have Max 8 and Max 9 aircraft with the updated software tied to this glitch in their fleets. Roblox — Shares of the gaming platform provider tumbled 6% after Jefferies downgraded the stock from hold, noting that it sees "pressures ahead." "The 30% run in the stock post Q2 results reflects an overly optimistic view of the 12mo Bookings trajectory," analyst James Heaney wrote. The firm anticipates the improvement in U.S. and Canada user and bookings growth will take longer and be more costly than the market expects. Kodiak Sciences — Shares rocketed about 170% after the biotech company announced that its experimental eye treatments Zenkuda and KSI-501 met primary endpoints in a Phase 3 study in patients with wet age-related macular degeneration. Cybersecurity stocks — Cybersecurity plays jumped Monday. Late last week, The New York Times reported that OpenAI's artificial intelligence accessed publicly available data from the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Census Bureau. The Global X Cybersecurity ETF (BUG) gained more than 1%. Shares of Palo Alto Networks advanced 4%, and shares of CrowdStrike jumped 3%. AI build-out stocks — Shares of companies tied to the AI build-out effort tumbled after news of OpenAI's latest agent escape and the company's move to pause training of its newest models. Shares of photonics companies Lumentum and Coherent dropped more than 5%. Shares of specialty glass and fiber company Corning slid 3%, and shares of Micron Technology lost 2%. Meta Platforms — The hyperscaler's stock slipped almost 4% following an almost 13% gain last week amid a series of announcements related to its personal AI agent Muse. Meta's fall on Monday came as stocks related to the AI trade broadly sold off. Newmont — The gold miner's stock fell more than 4% as the precious metal declined 3%. Higher global bond yields, including the 10-year U.S. Treasury note yield crossing 5.2%, are weakening demand for non-interest-bearing assets. Energy stocks — U.S. oil prices were off their session highs but remained elevated at about $93 per barrel. Shares of Exxon Mobil and Chevron both were higher by 1%. Airlines — Higher oil prices sent major airlines' stocks lower as investors digested the implications for jet fuel costs. Shares of United Airlines and American Airlines slipped more than 2% each, while Delta Air Lines ' stock was off by nearly 2%. Nvidia — While chipmakers broadly declined as tech stocks were lower to start the week, with the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) off 2%, Nvidia's stock outperformed and was up 2%. On Monday, the company announced new AI safety software and a $150 billion increase to its stock buyback program. Other chipmakers like Marvell Technology and Advanced Micro Devices started the week down 3%. — CNBC's Nick Wells and Darla Mercado contributed to this story.

headlines.article_text: Meta hires MongoDB CEO CJ Desai for enterprise unit Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points MongoDB CEO CJ Desai is joining Meta Platforms as its chief enterprise platform officer. Desai will lead the company's new business unit called Meta Enterprise Platform and report to Mark Zuckerberg. Dev Ittycheria, who stepped down from his role as CEO of MongoDB in November, was named interim president and CEO. In this article MDB META Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 0:49 00:49 Meta hires MongoDB CEO CJ Desai, sending shares of data services company down Squawk on the Street MongoDB CEO CJ Desai is joining Meta Platforms as its chief enterprise platform officer and will report directly to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg . Desai, who was in his role at MongoDB for less than a year, will be leading the social media giant's new Meta Enterprise Platform for businesses, according to a release. The new platform will initially prioritize a suite of tools that includes its new Muse agent, business agent and a coding tool. Meta plans to use "strengths that few other companies have: advanced models, leading agents, large-scale infrastructure, and years of working closely with many businesses," Zuckerberg wrote in the release. The news sent shares of MongoDB plummeting 18%. Meta's stock declined about 4%. The MongoDB board named Dev Ittycheria as interim president and CEO. Desai took over from Ittycheria, who served as CEO for 11 years, in November 2025. Desai previously spent a year as president of product and engineering at Cloudflare . He also worked as operating chief at enterprise software maker ServiceNow. Desai's transition comes as Meta undergoes a massive pivot, betting big on new artificial intelligence products and services for its enterprise customers. Amid this transition, investors have demanded a payoff from the company's hefty AI investments on new infrastructure and tools. The social media giant's push into the AI agent market with its Muse personal AI assistant has seen a rush of consumer demand, overtaking OpenAI's ChatGPT as the leading free iOS app. At the same time, a heated battle is unfolding in both Washington and Silicon Valley after top AI researchers and tech leaders, such as Anthropic 's Dario Amodei, called for a development slowdown amid mounting concerns over AI safety. MongoDB has shed nearly a quarter of its market value in 2026. headlines.title: Whole Foods co-founder shares tips for launching a successful second act: 'I'm relearning some lessons'
headlines.summary: John Mackey is learning that what helped him build Whole Foods Market into a multibillion-dollar business can help him in his second act, but only if he's patient.
headlines.article_text: Whole Foods co-founder's tips for launching a successful second act Skip Navigation Related Stories Work Job candidates need these 2 AI-proof traits to get hired, says Canva's chief people officer: It's a 'baseline' Success I manage Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library in Cincinnati—the No. 1 lesson she taught me about success Work Do these 5 things before the end of your summer internship, career experts say Health and Wellness From booksmaxxing to looksmaxxing: Why the trends concern mental health experts Work Don't just follow your passion—'successful and happy' people prioritize 2 things in their careers, says expert Lucy Nicholson | Reuters Whole Foods founder and former co-CEO, John Mackey sold Whole Foods to Amazon for $13.7 billion in 2017. Then he stepped away in 2022 after five years of leading his business through that transition to new ownership. "A lot of my friends just thought I'd retire," says Mackey, whose net worth at the time of the sale, Forbes estimated , clocked in at more than $75 million. "I have all of this money. I don't have to do anything," says the 73-year-old entrepreneur. And yet he says he has more to give. "I just think everybody needs to create value for other people, and I still can." That follow-up venture: Love.Life, a health and wellness club he opened in Los Angeles in 2024. Dubbed a "longevity club" by Mackey and his team, Love.Life offers a wide range of services, from fitness facilities and a health-food cafe to tailored nutrition plans and primary care medical treatments. It's not cheap: Memberships cost anywhere from $400 per month to $28,500 per year, depending on the level of services and perks clients want. While Love.Life declined to share specific membership figures with CNBC Make It, Mackey is candid about his frustration that his latest venture hasn't taken off as quickly as he'd hoped. He acknowledges that team-building and learning how best to meet your clients' specific needs are processes that take time for any new business. Mackey can also look back on Whole Foods' long path to nationwide success as something of a road-map that he hopes Love.Life can eventually emulate. "The long-term vision is just like we did with Whole Foods," Mackey says. "It took us 14 years to get to 12 stores, and then when I retired we were [over 500]... So, Love.Life has a similar ladder to climb." Undeterred, here are the lessons Mackey is holding dear in round two of his entrepreneurial journey. Don't forget to be patient The first lesson Mackey offers for anyone looking to pull off a successful second act is that patience is even more essential when you've already become accustomed to success. "Some of the lessons that I knew when I was younger, I've had to relearn," Mackey says. One of those lessons is how intentional leaders need to be about building a new corporate culture from the ground up — one that revolves around a commonly held purpose or mission. Employees are best motivated by a leader who "can take the passion that you feel and articulate it in purpose statements and vision," Mackey says. It's an approach he admits he's still fine-tuning with a planned "makeover" that will include updated messaging, based on Mackey's vision while also incorporating customer feedback, to be literally displayed on the walls of Love.Life's club "to get that purpose codified and explicit so people can see it and be reinforced all the time," he says. Learn, and re-learn, from your mistakes Another piece of advice he has for second-act entrepreneurs: Remain willing to learn from your own mistakes. That's true whether you're learning from a new mistake, or re-learning old lessons, he notes. "I'm relearning some lessons that, unfortunately, I should have learned the first time [at Whole Foods]," Mackey says. "So, I'm making some new mistakes, but I'm making a lot fewer mistakes in general just because it's like, 'Ah, we tried that [at Whole Foods]. That is not a good idea. We're not going to do that.'" Invite feedback and act on it Companies also need to be constantly talking to their customers to learn which aspects of the business are working, and which need to be tweaked. "They're telling you what they like and they don't like all the time," he says. "[Customers] vote with their feet. They vote with what they choose to do. And when they come to Love.Life you have to be alert and paying attention." Hire the best, learn from the rest Another area where leaders need to be constantly paying attention to past mistakes is hiring employees, Mackey adds. Building a talented and motivated team is essential to any business' success. Mackey says he tends to follow the advice of former Apple co-founder Steve Jobs, who advised managers to only hire "A players [who] want to hire more A players," rather than "settling for B and C players." "You field the best team that you can, but you're always looking to upgrade… and you have to have a high standard to do that," says Mackey, noting that building a team of the best employees requires first learning from past hiring mistakes. "You learn by hiring B-listers, and then you can recognize them," he says. Show your team they count Mackey's final key factor for a successful second act is that the best leaders are those who use genuine recognition to motivate employees' passion for the company mission. Employees who display an authentic passion for the business are found to be the most productive and are most effective at winning over clients and customers, Mackey says. Love.Life borrows a tradition from Whole Foods where meetings end with verbal "appreciations," where managers and team members share positive feedback with one another. The key: The sentiments must be genuine, Mackey adds: "People know the difference between an authentic, caring appreciation and somebody that's blowing smoke up their butts," he says. "Authentic appreciations [are] good for the giver and good for the receiver." When employees genuinely believe in the purpose of the business and feel sincerely valued by their leaders, they are typically happier, more productive and are also less likely to leave for another job, career experts say . "People want two things: they want purpose and they want love," Mackey adds. "If you do these two things, no one's ever going to want to quit your company."
